newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: FEATURE - Ivory Coast has sweet dreams of cocoa factories.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Ivory Coast has sweet dreams of cocoa factories.

text.p: Ivory Coast, the world's largest cocoa producer, has put expansion of processing capacity at the top of its agenda for talks with world chocolate representatives on Friday.

But now that a recent industry stampede to build factories in the West African country is slowing, donors and some industry analysts are questioning whether world demand, or simply government tax sweeteners, lie behind the appetite for factory building.
"Our view is that if people want to come without subsidies it is a good thing," says one donor organisation backing a $150 million World Bank agricultural loan to Ivory Coast in place since 1995.

"But there are higher energy costs and large transport distances if you are based here. Will the market absorb that without the government paying subsidies and is the opportunity cost greater than the benefit?"
Ivory Coast wants to create jobs while boosting value added to export as it diversifies its agriculture-based economy into commodities processing, mining and energy sectors.
EXPANDING PROCESSING CAPACITY

Ivory Coast's commodities minister, Guy-Alain Emmanuel Gauze, said on June 13 that plans to build cocoa factories in Ivory Coast will take national processing capacity to 360,000 tonnes in 1997/98 (Oct-Sept).
Four factories, the largest recently absorbed by a world conglomerate, already process up to 150,000 tonnes a year.
"Any factory needs some sort of subsidy but somewhere there also needs to be an edge," said one industry observer, pointing to failed processing plants in Ecuador and Brazil.
"I don't think it (factories) will do Ivory Coast any good," he said, adding that a factory costing $20 million could earn back the same amount in five years on trading opportunities and then close.
"When the subsidies are over things look very different," he said, adding that a branded item or a foreign exchange advantage could help.

The firmest indication of continuing industry confidence came in May when the French chocolate manufacturer CEMOI told Reuters it was going ahead with a 50,000-tonne capacity factory near Abidjan. CEMOI has received an undisclosed incentive package.
"There is some compensation from Ivory Coast for setting up which is quite interesting," the firm's director told Reuters in May. "We are also looking at markets in China."
Ivory Coast wants to process 50 percent of annual production locally by 2000.

That ambition was given a boost in June by Callebaut-Barry -- the world's largest cocoa producer formed in the 1996 merger of Swiss Callebaut AG and France's Cacao Barry -- which already has three Ivorian factories.

The finished chocolate and chocolate coatings giant said it had plans for raising Ivorian capacity, possibly by building a new plant. But no details have emerged and local managers have said Ivorian factory profits are unimpressive.
OTHER PROJECTS DELAYED
A raft of other projects, some of which have been formally submitted to the government, have recently been put on hold or become bogged down in negotiations.

U.S.-based Cargill told Reuters in Abidjan that a decision on its plans for building a 60,000-tonne plant with Ivorian exporter SICC was now unlikely until October. A decision had previously been slated for July at the latest.

Analysts say the French group Orebi has put plans for a 25-75,000-tonne plant in Ivory Coast's second port of San Pedro on the backburner. The group, with partners Ivorian exporter ERAF and Dutch group Nederland, had already selected a site.

China's growing sweet tooth is also being targeted by a Sino-French-Ivorian group, STF-CI, which has submitted a plan to build a 15-25,000-tonne cocoa processing plant in Ivory Coast -- with exports destined for China.
And a Sino-French partnership of France's Touton SA and Chinese Factory owner Shanghai Collin met in March to discuss plans for a processing plant in Ivory Coast.
But both Chinese projects remain on the drawing board.
GROWTH IN CONSUMPTION

In May, a report by British-based trader ED and F Man saw world 1996/97 (Oct/Sept) cocoa consumption growing by between three and four percent to 2,795,000 tonnes -- with significant bean grindings growth in Asia and Africa.
Cocoa analysts expect a trend of exporting Ivorian beans and cocoa liquor (shelled and ground cocoa beans) to France to increase.
Callebaut-Barry has chocolate plants near Paris and a group called OGS Invest says it will build a 60,000-tonnes bean processing plant near Rouen, starting in 1997.
French year-on-year imports of Ivorian beans rose to more than 25,000 tonnes in January-March 1997 against nearer 17,000 in the same 1996 period.

Elsewhere, Ivory Coast's exporting giant Octide, owner of Jean-Abile Gal, has held discussions with a Dutch Group on buying a bean processing plant in the Netherlands. Octide was beaten by U.S.-based Arthur Daniel Midland to a recent sell-off of shares in Ivory Coast's second largest processor, UNICAO.
If all Ivory Coast's dreams came true, domestic processing could reach around 400,000 tonnes by 2000, assuming all the proposed factories are built on time. Most take a year to build.
But that would leave it well short of its 50 percent target after a record 1.2-million-tonne crop in 1995/96 (Oct-Sept). This year's harvest is likely to be only a little below that level.
Crop analysts see salutary lessons in Nigeria's experience.
"In Nigeria they have about four factories that are doing nothing," he said. "They could not get beans cheaply enough as other buyers were bidding higher prices."

"Good Nigerian cocoa, if you can get it, is still in demand but in the last couple of years I doubt they have processed more than 20-30,000 tonnes..." from factories with a total capacity of 40-50,000 tonnes, said the analyst.
